newsitem.title: BELGIUM: SOCCER-SCIFO FEELING AT HOME BACK AT ANDERLECHT.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-SCIFO FEELING AT HOME BACK AT ANDERLECHT.

text.p: Enzo Scifo, Belgium's undisputed number one soccer player of the past 10 years, has returned to his old club Anderlecht to fulfil a dream.
Scifo, who took a drastic cut in salary to move from Monaco, said: "I had foreseen this return in my career planning. When I left (in 1987), I knew I'd come back.
"My heart belongs here, it's a love story between Anderlecht and me. I'm becoming alive again."
Scifo, born in Belgium to Italian parents, made his Anderlecht debut when he was just 17 and after four successful seasons joined Inter Milan in 1987.
He struggled to make an impact on Serie A and a disappointing spell with Bordeaux in France followed.
However, he rekindled his career at Auxerre before returning to Italy with Torino in 1991 and then Monaco two years later.
Scifo, now 31, said he wanted to return to Anderlecht at the height of his powers and dismissed suggestions he was just seeking a comfortable end-of-career spell.
"I didn't want to wait too long. Now I still have all my skills, I'm still in super shape," he said. "If I wanted to please supporters here at Anderlecht I just had to come back now.
"I've made enormous concessions to come here. Everybody knows I had quite a good financial deal at Monaco."
Scifo agreed to join Anderlecht in February as the club were struggling after a series of mediocre performances and off-pitch woes.
His arrival in time for the new season, on a three-year contract, helped convince seven other players, including former Monaco team mate Dan Petersen of Denmark, to sign for the Brussels club.

Anderlecht manager Michel Verschueren paid tribute to Scifo by saying he had single-handedly sparked a metamorphosis at the club, which is now aiming for a 25th league title after finishing a disappointing fourth last season.

Scifo, who has been a creative midfielder throughout his career, will assume a more defensive role this season and will be expected to back up and feed Swedish international midfielder Par Zetterberg.
"With Zetterberg's presence I really thought this would be the ideal moment to move into that (more defensive) position," Scifo said.
Belgian media, however, predicted that Belgium captain Scifo and Anderlecht skipper Zetterberg would both be vying for the limelight and were not at all complementary.
"It's not my ambition to be bigger than him (Zetterberg). There will not be any problem," Scifo said.

For Scifo, who by the age of 14 had earned the nickname "Little Pele" after some prodigious scoring feats for his first club La Louviere, time appeared to have been standing still at Anderlecht during his 10-year absence.
"Nothing much has changed, management is about the same, the stadium is the same, the club's ambitions are the same. I don't feel like a fish out of water here," he said.
Even new coach Rene Vandereycken is an old acquaintance, having played alongside Scifo for Belgium in the 1986 World Cup.
"As a player he was talented and tactically very cunning," said Scifo of his new boss.
Scifo has since played in two more World Cups and is keen to add a fourth next year.
Belgium and The Netherlands are joint leaders in their qualifying group and their September 6 match in Rotterdam should determine who will claim the one automatic place for the finals in France.
"I believe more than ever that we can qualify and that we are capable of beating the Dutch at home," Scifo said. "More than ever I believe in it. I'll do anything to get to the finals."
Scifo's appetite is a sharp as ever, despite a professional career already spanning 15 years. He said he could not yet envisage the end of his career.
"It's impossible for me to think about it," he said.
